item.title: Insufficient evidence to charge 11 police officers
item.description: The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) has found there is insufficient evidence to lay criminal charges against 11 police officers investigated over allegations linked to leaked Viber messages and alleged corrupt conduct. item.content:encoded:
The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP) has found there is insufficient evidence to lay criminal charges against 11 police officers investigated over allegations linked to leaked Viber messages and alleged corrupt conduct.

In a statement issued today, the ODPP confirmed it had completed its legal assessment of 11 police investigation dockets referred by the Fiji Police Force following allegations arising from a series of Facebook posts containing screenshots of Viber messages.

Those implicated included officers from the Narcotics Bureau.

The complaint alleged the officers had received corrupt benefits or bribes and had engaged in discussions relating to illicit drug activities.

Following what the Acting Director of Public Prosecutions described as a careful review of all available evidence, the ODPP concluded that the evidence currently available does not meet the threshold required to prosecute any of the officers.

“As a result of a careful review and assessment of all the available evidence, the Acting Director of Public Prosecutions has determined that there is currently insufficient evidence to institute charges against any of the 11 police officers,” the statement said.

The ODPP has now returned the investigation files to the Fiji Police Force together with recommendations for further investigations and identified additional matters for police to consider.

The Office said the matter remains open and could be reassessed if investigators uncover new evidence.

“The ODPP will conduct a further review of the files should further investigations yield new or sufficient evidence that establishes or supports the commission of any criminal offence,” the statement added.

The decision means no charges will be filed against the officers at this stage, pending any further investigations by the Fiji Police Force.

item.title: ‘Sugar mills’ future being assessed’
item.description: The possible privatisation of the Fiji Sugar Corporation’s (FSC) mills remains part of ongoing discussions as Government reviews the future structure of Fiji’s sugar industry. Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica said no final decision had been made on the future ownership or operation of the mills, with evaluations still underway.
item.content:encoded:
The possible privatisation of the Fiji Sugar Corporation’s (FSC) mills remains part of ongoing discussions as Government reviews the future structure of Fiji’s sugar industry.

Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica said no final decision had been made on the future ownership or operation of the mills, with evaluations still underway.

His comments followed a meeting at Takia Hotel involving Government stakeholders and the committee tasked with examining challenges facing the sugar sector.

The discussions focused on key issues affecting the industry, including restructuring options, improving profitability and determining the most effective model for the future management of the mills.

Mr Kamikamica confirmed that privatisation remained one of the options being considered.

“It’s part of the process and right now it’s probably too early to say what’s going to be done,” he said.

He said a major restructure of the sugar industry was certain as Government worked towards creating a more sustainable and profitable sector for farmers, workers and other stakeholders.

item.title: Call for sugar rethink
item.description: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says Fiji must take a fresh look at the future of the sugar industry, urging a shift from exporting raw sugar to developing value-added products and strengthening regional markets. Speaking on the industry’s future, Mr Rabuka said Fiji could no longer rely solely on the international demand for raw sugar, including exports to the European Union.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says Fiji must take a fresh look at the future of the sugar industry, urging a shift from exporting raw sugar to developing value-added products and strengthening regional markets.

Speaking on the industry’s future, Mr Rabuka said Fiji could no longer rely solely on the international demand for raw sugar, including exports to the European Union.

“What is the future of sugar – is it just to provide raw sugar for export, or do we now have to look at developing value-adding to our sugar,” he said.

He said Fiji had the opportunity to create greater economic returns by investing in downstream processing and refining sugar for regional markets.

“This can provide a new direction for the industry while allowing Fiji to make greater use of its sugar production.”

Mr Rabuka’s comments come as Government, farmers and industry stakeholders continue to examine ways of improving the long-term sustainability of one of Fiji’s most important agricultural sectors.

He said greater emphasis should be placed on creating more value from sugar production rather than depending primarily on raw sugar exports.

The Prime Minister also acknowledged the ongoing challenges facing sugar production in the Western Division and said Government may eventually consider gradually reducing production there if conditions continued to deteriorate.

However, he stressed there were no immediate plans to close the sugar industry in the West.

His comments followed remarks by The People’s Alliance party president Ratu Josefa Dimuri, who suggested Government should consider scaling down the sugar industry in the West and place greater emphasis on expanding production in the North.

Mr Rabuka said the North held significant potential for sugar production as well as other agricultural activities.

He added that if sugar production in the West became increasingly difficult, it could be phased down gradually while alternative agricultural industries were developed alongside it.

“We can slowly tone it down and have it replaced at the same time.”

Mr Rabuka said any future transition would need to protect the interests of landowners and operators while ensuring that new agricultural opportunities were created to support rural communities.

item.title: Kamikamica cites abuse in Walesi report
item.description: A GOVERNMENT investigation into Walesi found allegations of abuse of office and procedures not being followed, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says. Mr Kamikamica said the findings had raised concerns over the way some matters were handled and whether money had been properly used.
item.content:encoded:
A GOVERNMENT investigation into Walesi found allegations of abuse of office and procedures not being followed, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says.

Mr Kamikamica said the findings had raised concerns over the way some matters were handled and whether money had been properly used.

“There was some abuse of office, as far as I’m concerned, in the report. Abuse of office and procedures not followed.”

He said the findings had been referred to the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC), which would need to verify the allegations.

He said FICAC should follow through with the findings and establish whether the concerns raised in the report were correct and whether allegations of wrongdoing occurred.

He also raised concerns about the use of public funds in the process.

“There’s quite a bit of money that was probably not properly used in the process.”

item.title: ‘Report still with FICAC’
item.description: AN AUDIT report into the management and operations of Walesi has remained with the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) for about a year, with Government maintaining that it has completed its role and the next steps now rest entirely with the country’s anti-corruption watchdog. item.content:encoded:
AN AUDIT report into the management and operations of Walesi has remained with the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) for about a year, with Government maintaining that it has completed its role and the next steps now rest entirely with the country’s anti-corruption watchdog.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industry, Commerce, Business Development and Public Enterprise Manoa Kamikamica confirmed the report was still with FICAC and said the commission was responsible for determining whether criminal investigations or prosecutions would follow.

“All the findings have been submitted to FICAC, so it’s really FICAC’s chance to deal with it,” Mr Kamikamica said.

Asked when the public could expect charges, he said the Government could not interfere with the work of an independent investigative body.

“The report has been sitting with them for easily, I think, 12 months, but maybe more.”

Mr Kamikamica said the findings first needed to be assessed and verified by FICAC before any further action could be taken.

“The Government has completed its part by submitting the findings to the commission.”

The report is understood to have examined both the technical implementation of Fiji’s Digital Terrestrial Television (DTT) project and the financial management of Walesi Pte Ltd.

In December 2024, FICAC confirmed receiving the audited report from Mr Kamikamica and said the referral would be treated as a priority while investigations proceeded in accordance with its established processes and procedures.

Then commissioner Barbara Malimali also appointed a special taskforce to investigate the matter after the Office of the Auditor-General’s Special Audit identified significant concerns surrounding the multimillion-dollar project.

The audit found that Government had disbursed a total of $123.6million between 2015 and 2022 to fund the Digital Terrestrial Television project and the operations of Walesi.

Among the findings were concerns that approximately $80million, or about 68 per cent of total expenditure, reflected weak governance, poor planning or possible misuse of public funds. Auditors also questioned $9.3million in payments that lacked sufficient documentation to verify their purpose or compliance with procurement requirements.

The report further highlighted concerns over more than 200,000 Walesi receiver boxes that had reportedly become technologically obsolete within a year of procurement, raising questions over planning, value for money and long-term project management.

The technical assessment also identified operational shortcomings, including the absence of key operating licences during parts of the project’s implementation, while naming several private entities whose dealings with Walesi were considered significant enough to warrant further investigation.

Despite the scale of the audit findings, no charges have been announced.

Whether the audit findings ultimately lead to criminal prosecutions will now depend on FICAC’s assessment of the evidence and whether it determines that offences under Fiji’s anti-corruption laws can be substantiated.

item.title: $40k fine for violating ban
item.description: A HEFTY penalty is what villagers in Yasawa and the Mamanucas could face if they do not adhere to the restrictions of a biosecurity control to prevent the spread of a Tongan fruit fly that was detected in the two maritime groups. The government restriction was made official in a gazette from the Ministry of Agriculture which ordered the controls be imposed on villagers travelling from Yasawa and M
item.content:encoded:
A HEFTY penalty is what villagers in Yasawa and the Mamanucas could face if they do not adhere to the restrictions of a biosecurity control to prevent the spread of a Tongan fruit fly that was detected in the two maritime groups.

The government restriction was made official in a gazette from the Ministry of Agriculture which ordered the controls be imposed on villagers travelling from Yasawa and Mamanuca to Viti Levu.

Produce that have been listed as restricted include mango, guava, papaya, breadfruit, citrus, chilli, tomato, eggplant, capsicum, cucumber, starfruit and other homegrown fruit and vegetables.

Under the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji Act 2008, anyone caught illegally transporting banned fruits or hosting materials from the Yasawa and Mamanuca groups faces immediate legal prosecution with individuals facing a fine of up to $40,000 and companies a maximum of $200,000.

Naviti district spokesperson Meciusela Vuli said villagers had been observing the restriction since the first few months of 2026.

“The Ministry of Agriculture team came to our seven villages, they carried out awareness for our people, and they put up traps for this fruit fly,” Mr Vuli said.

“Right now, we can’t take any type of fruit including uto (breadfruit), vudi (plantain), pawpaw, mangoes, moli (lemon) and vegetables.

“So, we are listening and we have been reminding our people to follow the law.”

He said while majority of villagers had been adhering to the restrictions, some had been fined.

“We had a villager whose child was carrying a piece of dawa in their bag.

“They found it at the wharf when the family arrived in Lautoka. They were fined on the spot, $1000. After that everyone feared they could be fined too so we made sure we followed what is being said.”

Mr Vuli said checkpoints had been set up at offloading points where government officers had been checking bags and produce.

Kese Village headman Rusiate Buli said livelihoods had not been adversely affected by the restrictions.

“Most of us that live on the island live off what we plant and what we get from the sea,” he said.

“A lot of us also work in the nearby resorts. What we take to Lautoka is mainly seafood to sell so we cannot say we have been affected.

“What I am seeing now is that the restriction is in a gazette. That is a law now which we have to follow or face a fine.”

item.title: Moves to integrate villages into city councils
item.description: THE government is moving to formally integrate villages located near municipal boundaries into town and city council governance structures to give residents a voice in local administration, says Housing and Local Government Minister Maciu Nalumisa. While most of these communities already receive municipal services, Mr Nalumisa said they had historically been excluded from council decision-making.
item.content:encoded:
THE government is moving to formally integrate villages located near municipal boundaries into town and city council governance structures to give residents a voice in local administration, says Housing and Local Government Minister Maciu Nalumisa.

While most of these communities already receive municipal services, Mr Nalumisa said they had historically been excluded from council decision-making.

Mr Nalumisa did not confirm whether these communities would be paying town or city rates but Lautoka Board of Special Administrators chairman Taitusi Rasoki did say that discussions were still in the proposal stage as far as Lautoka City was concerned.

“They don’t know what’s happening, they don’t have a say in the administration, the governance of the council,” Mr Nalumisa said.

“So that’s the basic reason why we are involving all these villages that are closer to the municipal boundaries.”

To address the financial impact of town rate assessments on these communities, the government is currently providing waste collection subsidies.

“The ministry is also collaborating with the Ministry of iTaukei Affairs for them to assess the payment of rates for all these villages.”

Nawaka district representative Panapasa Driu Qoro said basic services such as rubbish collection had been implemented by the Nadi Town Council.

“I think we will be included in this local government elections, even the settlements and surrounding areas,” he said.

Mr Driu said developments within Nadi Town had expanded to include nearby villages since 2020, therefore it was only right that these communities be allowed to vote in the local government elections.

item.title: Judge adjourns drug case
item.description: THE High Court in Lautoka yesterday adjourned a case of three individuals accused of importing nearly half a tonne of methamphetamine. This, after the State requested additional time to obtain transcribed versions of their caution interviews.
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court in Lautoka yesterday adjourned a case of three individuals accused of importing nearly half a tonne of methamphetamine.

This, after the State requested additional time to obtain transcribed versions of their caution interviews.

Chan Mooi Sing, Kalokalo Mataunidilo, and Mereanj Canisiga appeared before Justice Sunil Sharma yesterday, facing joint charges of unlawful importation and possession of 491.6 kilograms of meth.

It is alleged the illicit consignment arrived on January 6 on a flight from Malaysia through Singapore.

State lawyer Laisiasa Baleilevuka told the court that transcribed records of the caution interviews conducted with the accused remained pending.

He sought further time to finalise the transcripts and serve them on the defence.

Defence lawyer Mosese Naivalu, representing Ms Sing, raised no objection to the State’s requests, but told the court his client was developing a fever and sought leave to visit a hospital.

Addressing the oral application, Justice Sharma said the Women’s Remand Centre at Natabua had sufficient medical personnel to attend to inmates.

He said inmates must follow standard facility protocol by informing the officer on duty.

Justice Sharma adjourned the matter to August 26 for mention.
